newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines puts pressure on pilots.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines puts pressure on pilots.

text.p: Faced with the threat of a strike, American Airlines has decided to force its pilots into either dropping their wage demands or staging a walkout in February when traffic is low, company officials said Monday.
"If we are going to take a strike, February is the time to take it because it is our slowest time of the year," said one company official, asking not to be identified.

He said the carrier, which is owned by Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp., chose to bring the long-running contract dispute to a head after pilots last week rejected a tentative four-year contract reached last September.
Chief Executive Officer Robert Crandall warned American's employees on Monday that a pilots' strike was a very real possibility, and put the blame on the union.

"A week ago, we were busy planning the configuration and deployment of new airplanes, the refurbishment of our existing fleet, service improvements for the year 1997 and a return to modest growth," he said in a letter to employees. "Today, we are faced with two disastrous alternatives -- unacceptably high costs or cessation of operations."
The carrier said Friday it would accept an offer of binding arbitration from the National Mediation Board, but insisted that the pilots also agree to the offer by 8 a.m. Wednesday.

If the pilots' union does not respond by then, Crandall said, the airline will itself decline binding arbitration. That would force the start of a 30-day "cooling off" period of intensive negotiations.

At the end of those 30 days, if no agreement was struck, the Allied Pilots Association would be free to strike while American could declare a lockout and unilaterally implement new pay and work rules.
Both sides agree that the outcome of such an all-out confrontation would define the airline's future.
Union officials said Monday they still hoped the two sides could renew negotiations without binding arbitration, and said they had sent the airline their latest proposal.

"The pilots would like to avoid confrontation, but they are more than willing to strike over these contract issues. The ball is in American's court. If they want to negotiate, we'll negotiate," union spokesman Wally Pitts said.
But he said the two sides were far apart and that he was not optimistic. "I think Crandall wants a confrontation. It appears he wants to fight it out," Pitts said.
The union's proposal was unlikely to ease the pressure.

After last week's rejection of the tentative agreement, which would have given them a 5 percent pay raise over four years, the pilots are now demanding more than 11 percent and justify it by pointing to American's record profits in recent months.

They also are demanding that the carrier drop all plans to allow its American Eagle unit to fly regional jets. The commuter airline employs pilots from a different union, and Airline Pilots Association members said they believed American would try to turn more of its short-haul routes over to American Eagle, thereby threatening their jobs.

Airline officials said the pilots' demands are excessive and would cripple the company, threatening its plans for modest growth. That includes the huge aircraft order worth at least $6.5 billion which was placed with Boeing Co. two months ago but which has now been put on hold.

Above all else, airline management wants to prevent the union from dragging its feet in the months ahead and finally rejecting arbitration in May in order to set itself up for a strike in the summer, when traffic levels hit a peak.
"If we are going to get put on a 30-day clock (the "cooling-off" period before a strike), we want it in the first quarter," the company official said Monday.

But Pitts said a strike could be as effective in February as it is in June. He said the airline's fixed costs are the same all year and that summer strikes simply strand customers because other airlines are running full, while off-season strikes push customers to rival carriers.
"It really doesn't matter when you strike," Pitts said.
